newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia barley hinges on rain, plant - Grainco.
newsitem.headline: Australia barley hinges on rain, plant - Grainco.

text.p: Good rain over the next month and a sizeable winter feed barley plant could see significant tonnages appearing on the Australian market, Queensland grain co-operative Grainco Ltd said in its weekly market report.
Domestic feed barley prices remained stable over the past week in limited stock trading, trading manager Rob Brealey said.
Growers still holding barley stocks on farm continued to stand aside from the market for the time being, he said.

The export market remained quiet with only May-July business yet to be finalised by Chinese and South American buyers. Deferred values remained under some pressure with most buyers demanding premium specifications, he said.
Crop conditions in the northern hemisphere and planting conditions in Australia would dictate future market direction, he said.

Last week remained relatively quiet for the domestic sorghum market while volatility continued in the international market. The week saw some grower selling but tonnages remained relatively minor as growers continued to hold the largest share
of south Queensland production in storage.

The central Queensland crop continues to progress well, he said. Domestic values, however, had turned slightly more volatile given they more closely follow movements in the export market than south Queensland values.

Some uncertainty remains about the size of the central Queensland crop, with the opportunity there for some of the late planted crop to increase yields with timely rain and a favourable finish, he said.
Internationally, some risk premium was likely to be built into corn futures contracts until the market was more comfortable with the size of the corn crop, he said.

Domestic sorghum values finished last week about A$152.00 a tonne delivered Brisbane for prompt south Queensland sorghum, while in central Queensland values finished the week at about A$136.00 a tonne for June/July delivery.
South Queensland values continue to reflect the sizeable domestic premium the market is paying over international values, he said.
Australian cash cottonseed markets were maintaining a steady pace. Consumption activity has improved in the domestic market, while export business remains steady.
Demand was plentiful for seed on a prompt basis because of a slow start to the ginning season, he said.

Early reports were mixed on quality and yields, particularly for dryland crops. It was presently too early to tell whether this was indicative of the whole crop or whether it was a localised feature of the early Darling Downs crop in southern Queensland, he said.
Cottonseed prices last week softened a little from the previous week. Grower business was being transacted in the low A$130.00 a tonne range ex gin across Queensland.

Domestic Australian soybean values remained unchanged over the past week with sunflowers finishing at A$310.00 a tonne delivered Brisbane for April 1997 and A$315.00 a tonne delivered Newcastle for April 1997.

Central Queensland new crop black sunflower prices were around A$250.00-A$255.00 a tonne delivered central Queensland depot for May-July 1997. New crop soybean prices traded higher at A$414.00 a tonne delivered Brisbane, while canola traded at
A$335.00 a tonne delivered Moree for April 1997 delivery.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
